# Method: composite quality valuation + spread-quantile group placement

## Rendering (matches the recipe)
Each row was rendered exactly as `recipe/sft.py` trains it: plain ChatML
(`<|im_start|>{role}\n{content}<|im_end|>\n`, think blocks kept verbatim in every
assistant turn), truncated at `max_len` = 32768, with the loss mask on assistant
content + `<|im_end|>` only. All token statistics and the base-model NLL use this
rendering, so "truncated" and "assistant tokens" mean what they will mean in training.

## Per-row signals
Heuristic (computed on all 10,000 rows):
- **confirmed completion** — trajectory ends with the harness's "Are you sure you want
  to mark the task as complete?" prompt answered by `"task_complete": true` (strong
  proxy that the episode actually solved its task; 58% of rows).
- **task_complete at end** (weaker version, 64%).
- **truncated at 32768 tokens** (loses the resolution; 3.5% of rows) — heavy penalty.
- **warning rate** = harness format-warning turns / assistant turns (median 0.82 —
  ubiquitous, so used as a graded z-scored penalty, not a filter).
- **error-turn rate**, **JSON parse rate** of assistant replies (after stripping
  `<think>`), **duplicate-assistant-turn ratio** (flailing), **empty-command
  mid-trajectory rate** (stalling).
- **assistant tokens within the 32k window** (log, z-scored, small positive weight —
  more supervised tokens per row at fixed 1000 rows).

Model-based (inference-only forward passes of the base model):
- **mean NLL per assistant token** under the base Qwen3-4B, computed with the exact
  training rendering/mask. High NLL flags noisy / off-distribution / degenerate
  completions; a tiny penalty is also applied to extreme low-NLL outliers (trivially
  predictable text). The pass ran longest-rows-first and covered the 4,669 longest rows
  before the time budget forced a stop; unscored (shorter) rows get a neutral 0 z-score.

Composite score = 3·confirmed + 1·task_complete − 4·truncated − 1·z(warn_rate)
− 2·err_rate − 15·(1−json_rate) − 3·dup_asst − 1·empty_cmd_rate − 0.8·max(z_nll,0)
− 0.2·max(−z_nll−2,0) + 0.4·z(log assistant_tokens). Weights chosen so the
success/completeness signals dominate and format/coherence signals order rows within
those tiers.

## Group construction
All rows are ranked by the composite score, then groups are placed at **spread
quantiles** of the ranking (5,000 of 10,000 rows selected):

- **Group 1 = ranks 1–1000** (the headline set), with two diversity constraints applied
  greedily in score order: at most one row per identical task prompt, and at most 40
  rows (4%) per task-topic cluster (TF-IDF over the task description, k=100
  MiniBatchKMeans). Result: 100% confirmed completions, 0% truncated, lowest warning
  rate, broad task coverage.
- **Group 2 ≈ ranks 2000–3000, Group 3 ≈ 4500–5500, Group 4 ≈ 7000–8000,
  Group 5 ≈ 9000–10000** (the worst tail: 34% truncated, ~3% confirmed, highest NLL,
  most flailing).

Rationale: the primary objective (group 1 strength) depends only on the top band, so
group 1 takes the best rows with diversity de-duplication. For the ordering objective,
spacing the remaining groups across the full quality range of the pool maximizes the
expected gap between consecutive groups' post-training benchmark scores, making the
monotone ordering (Spearman → −1) robust to noise in both the valuation and the
benchmark — much more robust than adjacent rank bands (ranks 1–5000), which would make
groups 2–5 nearly indistinguishable since ~5,800 rows are "confirmed & untruncated".

Group means of the composite score: +4.40, +4.00, +2.90, −0.66, −3.55 (confirmed-end
fraction 1.00 / 1.00 / 0.99 / 0.01 / 0.03; truncation 0 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.34).

# Data-selection method

**Goal.** Rank all 10,000 terminal-agent SFT trajectories by expected downstream value,
select 5 disjoint groups of 1,000 so group 1 trains the best model and quality decreases
monotonically to group 5.

## Signals (per row)

**CPU-parsed trajectory quality** (each assistant turn is `<think>…</think>` + a JSON
command batch; each following user turn is environment feedback):

- **Outcome** — whether the final assistant turn declares `task_complete: true`
  (+2.0), `false` (−0.4), or is missing / cut off mid-task (−0.8). Dominant term:
  successful demonstrations teach task completion; unfinished ones teach meandering.
- **Format fidelity** — rate of environment `parsing errors` (−3.0/turn-rate),
  unparseable JSON after think-removal (−3.0), residual text between `</think>` and the
  JSON (−1.0), generic warnings (−0.3), missing `<think>` opener (+0.3 for all-present).
  The benchmark scores automated command execution, so training on responses the
  harness rejected is actively harmful.
- **Degenerate behavior** — identical consecutive command batches (loops, −2.0 rate),
  empty command batches without completion (−0.1 each), environment timeout warnings
  (−0.8).
- **Truncation** — rows exceeding the recipe's 32,768-token cutoff lose their tail
  (including the completion): penalty proportional to the fraction of assistant tokens
  lost, plus a flat term. Tokenization exactly mirrors the recipe (plain ChatML,
  think kept verbatim every turn, loss on assistant content + `<|im_end|>`).
- **Mild mid-length preference** — 0.15 · |log2(len/12k)|, keeping a length mix while
  avoiding the extremes (trivially short; long-wandering, which also correlate with
  failure).

**GPU signal (base-model NLL, inference only).** Mean NLL of the base Qwen3-4B on
assistant tokens over the first 8,192 tokens of each row in recipe format (78M tokens,
~43 min on the H100). Used as a band filter: strong penalty on the high tail
(z > 1.5 → noisy / off-distribution content) and a mild one on the very low tail
(z < −2 → trivial/repetitive, little to learn). Mid-band is preferred.

## Group assignment

Rows are ranked by the composite score. To make the group-index → score ordering
robust (Spearman → −1), groups are taken from **spaced windows** of the global ranking
rather than adjacent slices: g1 = ranks 1–1000, g2 from 1501, g3 from 3501, g4 from
6001, g5 from 9001 (the genuinely worst rows: 0% completions, 85% timeouts, 27%
truncated). Gaps between windows make each pairwise ordering hold even under scoring
noise, while g1 remains exactly the top-1000.

Diversity: within group 1 at most one row per task (hash of the task description);
looser caps for lower groups. Group 1 contains 1,000 unique tasks, all with clean
JSON in every turn, zero parse errors/loops/timeouts/truncation, 100% completions,
moderate length (mean 11.4k tokens, 8.3 assistant turns), and mid-band NLL.

## Verification

Spot checks: group-1 rows end with verified completions ("all 212 tests pass",
"verification passes"); group-5 rows are cut off mid-task. The CSV was validated:
5,000 unique indices in [0, 9999], exactly 1,000 per group_id ∈ {1..5}.

markdown:
# Method

## Setup
Config: `n_groups=5`, `group_size=1000`, `max_len=32768`, base model `./model`
(Qwen3-4B), dataset `./data/train.parquet` (10,000 rows, `messages` column,
OpenThoughts-Agent-style terminal-agent JSON-protocol trajectories: the
assistant replies each turn with `{"analysis", "plan", "commands", ...,
"task_complete"}` and the harness echoes back the next terminal state, with a
`WARNINGS:` line whenever the assistant's raw text didn't parse cleanly as
JSON).

Everything below is inference-only (no gradients/optimizer steps — enforced
by `guards/sitecustomize.py`) and never touches a held-out benchmark; all
signals come from the `messages` text itself and from base-model forward
passes over it.

## Signal 1 — text-mined trajectory-quality heuristics
For every row, parsed straight out of `messages`:
- **`complete`**: does the *last* assistant message contain
  `"task_complete": true`? This is the only outcome signal available (no
  ground-truth pass/fail label exists in the data), and empirically it is a
  strong one: completion rate falls from 81% at 5 turns to 11% at 35+ turns,
  and from 67% with zero JSON-format warnings to 31-46% once the assistant's
  output starts failing to parse as JSON (see below) — i.e. trajectories that
  reach a clean, deliberate stop are exactly the ones a downstream terminal
  agent should imitate.
- **`hard`**: count of *fatal* format failures the harness logged
  (`AUTO-CORRECTED: Extracted JSON from mixed content`, `No valid JSON object
  found`). These mark turns where the assistant's raw text needed manual
  repair before it was usable — training on such a turn teaches the model to
  reproduce malformed output. 12.9% of rows have `hard>0`.
- **`soft_rate`**: fraction of turns flagged `Extra text detected before JSON
  object`, i.e. the assistant wrote prose before the JSON instead of using a
  `<think>...</think>` block (verified by inspecting examples directly:
  trajectories that wrap reasoning in `<think>` tags essentially never trigger
  this warning; trajectories that ramble in plain prose before the JSON
  almost always do). This is a clean proxy for "disciplined, parseable output
  habit" and is strongly correlated with `complete` (soft_rate ~0.4-0.7 →
  95-99% completion; soft_rate ~0.9-1.0 → 33-44% completion).
- **`n_turns`**: number of assistant turns (a proxy for task-solving
  efficiency / not getting stuck; strongly anti-correlated with `complete`).
- **`rep`**: fraction of consecutive assistant turns that are near-duplicates
  (word-set Jaccard > 0.7) — catches stuck/looping behavior.
- **`truncated`**: whether the trajectory's token length (see below) exceeds
  `max_len`, meaning the fixed recipe's right-side truncation would cut off
  the end of the trajectory (often the concluding `task_complete` turn)
  during training.

## Signal 2 — base-model assistant-token loss (inference only)
The recipe trains with `assistant_only_loss=True` on a "plain ChatML,
`<think>` kept verbatim in every assistant turn" tokenization (its comments
describe this as the `allthink` tokenizer, reproducing the OpenThoughts-Agent
LLaMA-Factory `qwen3_nothink` template). We reproduce that exact
tokenization ourselves by wrapping every message as
`<|im_start|>{role}\n{content}<|im_end|>\n` and concatenating per-message
token ids (safe here since there are no system/tool roles and
`<|im_start|>`/`<|im_end|>` are single tokens, so this is byte-identical to
templating the whole conversation at once, just without the O(turns²)
re-templating cost).

For every row we ran one forward pass of the base model (bf16, SDPA, no
grad/no cache) over the first 4,096 tokens of this sequence (a time-budget
cap — full-length forward passes over the whole 10k-row, ~16.4k-tokens/row
pool would have taken ~5 hours; 4,096 tokens keeps the earliest turns, which
already carry a clear signal) and computed the mean cross-entropy loss over
assistant-token positions only (`mean_nll`).

We validated the direction empirically before using it: mean_nll is lower for
`complete==True` rows (1.27 vs 1.41 for incomplete) and lower for
`hard==0` rows (1.31 vs 1.37 for rows with a fatal format failure) — i.e.
lower assistant-token loss under the base model tracks the same notion of
"clean, successful, natural" trajectory as the text heuristics, so it is used
as a same-direction secondary/refinement term rather than a dominant one.

## Composite score and selection
For every one of the 10,000 rows:

```
composite = 3.0*complete
          - 4.0*min(hard, 5)
          - 1.5*zscore(soft_rate)
          - 0.6*zscore(log1p(n_turns))
          - 2.0*zscore(rep)
          - 1.5*truncated
          - 0.3*zscore(mean_nll)
```

Rows are sorted by `composite` descending; the top `n_groups*group_size =
5000` rows are kept and cut into 5 contiguous blocks of 1000 by rank
(block 1 = highest composite, block 5 = lowest of the selected set) →
`group_id`. This directly targets both objectives: group 1 is the single
best-scoring 1000-row subset (composite ≈ 6.6, ~100% `task_complete`, lowest
turn count, lowest format-warning rate, lowest assistant loss of any group),
and because groups are literal contiguous slices of one sorted list, the
ordering objective (group 1 > 2 > 3 > 4 > 5) holds by construction and was
confirmed on every input feature (mean `complete`: 1.00 / 1.00 / 0.999 /
0.999 / 0.975; mean `soft_rate`: 0.59 / 0.69 / 0.76 / 0.83 / 0.88; mean
`n_turns`: 5.2 / 6.7 / 8.3 / 11.3 / 14.8; mean `mean_nll`: 1.14 / 1.14 / 1.17
/ 1.28 / 1.43 — monotonic on every dimension). The excluded 5000 rows
(`hard>0`, incomplete, high-repetition/looping, or simply lower-ranked) are
left unused, as permitted.

## Scripts
- `scripts/build_spans.py` — manual ChatML tokenization + assistant-token
  mask per row (matches the recipe's `allthink` training format).
- `scripts/score_model.py` — base-model forward passes, assistant-token mean
  NLL per row (first 4096 tokens).
- `scripts/analyze_model_scores.py` — sanity-checks the sign/magnitude of the
  NLL signal against the text heuristics.
- `scripts/select_groups.py` — builds the composite score and writes
  `outputs/group_assignment.csv`.

For every row we ran one forward pass of the base model (bf16, SDPA, no grad/no cache) over the first 4,096 tokens of this sequence (a time-budget cap — full-length forward passes over the whole 10k-row, ~16.4k-tokens/row pool would have taken ~5 hours; 4,096 tokens keeps the earliest turns, which already carry a clear signal) and computed the mean cross-entropy loss over assistant-token positions only (mean_nll).

We validated the direction empirically before using it: mean_nll is lower for complete==True rows (1.27 vs 1.41 for incomplete) and lower for hard==0 rows (1.31 vs 1.37 for rows with a fatal format failure) — i.e. lower assistant-token loss under the base model tracks the same notion of "clean, successful, natural" trajectory as the text heuristics, so it is used as a same-direction secondary/refinement term rather than a dominant one.

Composite score and selection

For every one of the 10,000 rows:

composite = 3.0*complete
          - 4.0*min(hard, 5)
          - 1.5*zscore(soft_rate)
          - 0.6*zscore(log1p(n_turns))
          - 2.0*zscore(rep)
          - 1.5*truncated
          - 0.3*zscore(mean_nll)

Rows are sorted by composite descending; the top n_groups*group_size = 5000 rows are kept and cut into 5 contiguous blocks of 1000 by rank (block 1 = highest composite, block 5 = lowest of the selected set) → group_id. This directly targets both objectives: group 1 is the single best-scoring 1000-row subset (composite ≈ 6.6, ~100% task_complete, lowest turn count, lowest format-warning rate, lowest assistant loss of any group), and because groups are literal contiguous slices of one sorted list, the ordering objective (group 1 > 2 > 3 > 4 > 5) holds by construction and was confirmed on every input feature (mean complete: 1.00 / 1.00 / 0.999 / 0.999 / 0.975; mean soft_rate: 0.59 / 0.69 / 0.76 / 0.83 / 0.88; mean n_turns: 5.2 / 6.7 / 8.3 / 11.3 / 14.8; mean mean_nll: 1.14 / 1.14 / 1.17 / 1.28 / 1.43 — monotonic on every dimension). The excluded 5000 rows (hard>0, incomplete, high-repetition/looping, or simply lower-ranked) are left unused, as permitted.

Scripts

  • scripts/build_spans.py — manual ChatML tokenization + assistant-token mask per row (matches the recipe's allthink training format).
  • scripts/score_model.py — base-model forward passes, assistant-token mean NLL per row (first 4096 tokens).
  • scripts/analyze_model_scores.py — sanity-checks the sign/magnitude of the NLL signal against the text heuristics.
  • scripts/select_groups.py — builds the composite score and writes outputs/group_assignment.csv.

# Method

## Data
`data/train.parquet` (10,000 rows) holds Terminal-Bench-style agent rollouts: a system/task
prompt, then alternating assistant JSON turns (`analysis`/`plan`/`commands`/optional
`task_complete`) and user turns that echo terminal output (and, when the assistant's JSON
was malformed, a `"Previous response had warnings"` notice). A trajectory that sets
`task_complete: true` gets a final confirmation prompt ("Are you sure you want to mark the
task as complete? ...") before the episode ends — this mirrors the real terminal-bench
harness, so a trajectory that reaches and answers that confirmation is the strongest
available proxy for "the agent believed, and the harness accepted, that the task was
finished." There is no ground-truth pass/fail column, so all scoring is built from the
`messages` content itself plus base-model inference.

## Signals computed (inference-only, base model = `config.base_model`)
1. **Completion/success proxy** — parse each assistant turn's JSON. `success_component` =
   1.0 if the trajectory reached the completion-confirmation turn and re-confirmed
   `task_complete: true`, 0.7 if the final assistant turn merely claims `task_complete: true`
   without going through the confirmation step, else 0. This is the single biggest driver of
   SFT value: an unfinished/abandoned trajectory teaches the model to wander, not to solve.
2. **Format cleanliness** — fraction of assistant turns whose content parses as valid JSON
   containing the required `analysis`/`plan`/`commands` keys (`format_quality`), and a
   penalty (`warn_score`) based on how often the environment had to flag the previous
   response with a warning (extra text before/after JSON, missing newline on `keystrokes`,
   etc.), normalized per turn. Clean, schema-correct assistant turns are exactly what
   `assistant_only_loss` trains on, so noisy formatting directly hurts the trained policy's
   own output formatting (which the harness parses as JSON).
3. **Base-model fit (`loss_score`)** — for every row, the full conversation is rendered with
   `tokenizer.apply_chat_template` and tokenized once with offset mapping; assistant-token
   spans are located via the literal `<|im_start|>assistant\n ... <|im_end|>` markers (robust
   to the template's whitespace reformatting around `<think>` blocks). A single forward pass
   of the base model (bf16, no grad — forward-only, ~1.6 rows/s on the H100) gives per-token
   cross-entropy on assistant tokens only, matching the recipe's masked loss. The per-row
   mean loss is converted to a score peaked at the dataset's median loss and decaying with
   |z-score| (clipped at 3 IQRs): trajectories the base model already finds very easy
   (near-degenerate boilerplate) or very hard (garbled/anomalous, off-distribution) are both
   downweighted, keeping the "hard-but-learnable" middle.
4. **Length/truncation gate** — rows whose full chat-template token count exceeds `max_len`
   (32,768) are dropped (only 80/10,000): the recipe would truncate them, cutting off the
   loss on later turns and teaching an incomplete demonstration.
5. **Diversity (de-dup)** — task descriptions were hashed (full text, not just a prefix,
   since many rows share long boilerplate preambles but differ later); the ~90 exact
   duplicate rows are collapsed to their single best-scoring copy so no group wastes a slot
   on a literal repeat.

## Composite score
`composite = 0.45*success_component + 0.25*format_quality + 0.15*warn_score + 0.15*loss_score`

Success/completion dominates (it is the clearest signal of a trajectory worth imitating),
format cleanliness is weighted second (directly trains the harness-facing output format),
and warning-rate/loss-fit act as secondary quality and difficulty-calibration tie-breakers.

## Group assignment
All candidate rows (after the truncation gate and dedup) are sorted by `composite`
descending. The top 1,000 become group 1, the next 1,000 group 2, ..., down to group 5 —
giving a strictly decreasing mean composite score across groups (verified: group means
0.937 → 0.923 → 0.912 → 0.900 → 0.880) and, since de-duplication happens before slicing,
group 1 is built entirely from distinct tasks at the highest quality/success/format tier
available in the pool. 5,000 of the 9,830 eligible rows are used; the remaining rows
(lower composite score, or duplicates) are left unselected as instructed.

# Method

Goal: from the 10,000-row SFT candidate pool, select 5 disjoint groups of 1,000 rows
each such that group 1 (trained alone with the fixed recipe) is the strongest possible
1,000-row terminal-agent SFT set, and quality declines monotonically to group 5.

## 1. Understanding the data and the recipe

Each row is a multi-turn terminal-agent trajectory (Terminal-Bench-style): a system/task
prompt, then alternating assistant/user turns. The assistant must emit strict JSON
(`analysis`, `plan`, `commands`, optional `task_complete`) after a `<think>` block; the
harness (recorded in the following "user" turn) reports parser warnings
(`Extra text detected...`, `AUTO-CORRECTED: ...`, missing/unknown fields) when the JSON
was malformed. The recipe trains with `assistant_only_loss`, truncates at
`max_len=32768` tokens (right-truncation), for 7 epochs at lr 4e-5. Two facts drive the
whole approach:

- **What the model imitates during training is exactly what's in the `messages` column.**
  If a trajectory's assistant turns are malformed JSON, or the episode never actually
  finishes the task, the model learns to imitate *that* — directly hurting the
  benchmark, which scores whether the final tests pass.
- **Truncation silently deletes the tail.** ~0.8% of rows exceed 32,768 tokens; for
  those, the recipe's right-truncation cuts off the end of the trajectory — typically
  right where `task_complete` and the final summary live — so the model would never see
  the successful resolution, only an unfinished middle.

This reframes "predict SFT value per row" into a mostly *inference-free* problem:
almost all the signal is recoverable by parsing the trajectory's own structure and
harness feedback, which is exactly what the model will be trained to reproduce. A
(inference-only) base-model perplexity pass is added as a secondary, complementary
signal per the task's suggestion to combine signals.

## 2. Per-row signals (computed over all 10,000 rows)

1. **Task success proxy** — `last_task_complete`: does the final assistant JSON have
   `"task_complete": true`? (63.9% of rows overall.)
2. **Format compliance** — for every assistant turn, strip the leading `<think>` block
   and any markdown fences, then attempt to parse JSON (tolerating the "extra text"
   the harness itself tolerates); `json_ok_frac` = fraction of turns that parse into a
   dict with `analysis`/`plan`/`commands`.
3. **Harness-reported malformation** — counts of `AUTO-CORRECTED` (harness had to
   forcibly extract JSON from unparsable mixed content — a strong bad signal, present
   in ~12% of rows), `Extra text detected after JSON object`, and field-level issues
   (missing `duration`, unknown fields), all normalized per assistant turn.
4. **Token length under the real chat template** — `tokenizer.apply_chat_template`
   applied to the full conversation (base model's own tokenizer/template, since the
   recipe's custom "allthink" tokenizer isn't available to us) to get the exact token
   count relevant to the `max_len=32768` cutoff.
5. **Efficiency** — number of turns to reach completion. Empirically, within the full
   10k rows, turn count correlates negatively with `task_complete` (r=-0.34) and
   positively with autocorrect rate (r=+0.26) — longer, more meandering trajectories are
   measurably lower quality, not just harder tasks, so this is used as a real (mildly
   weighted) signal, not just a tie-breaker.
6. **Task-description clusters** — the human task prompt is extracted from each row and
   used to find near-duplicate tasks (same underlying question asked/attempted multiple
   times; 8,147 unique prompts out of 10,000, largest cluster size 7). Used for
   diversity, not correctness.

## 3. Base-model perplexity (inference-only, secondary signal)

For every row that passes the two hard filters below, one forward pass of the base
model (bf16, `no_grad`, single H100) computes mean per-token cross-entropy restricted to
assistant-turn tokens (assistant spans located via `<|im_start|>assistant...<|im_end|>`
offsets in the templated string; no gradients/optimizer steps, consistent with the
inference-only constraint). This gives a "how surprising is this trajectory's language
to the base model" score, used only as a mild penalty for the upper outlier tail (likely
garbled/degenerate content) and a small general preference for lower loss — a
complementary but intentionally low-weight signal, since success/format are far more
reliable given the ground-truth-like harness feedback available here.

## 4. Hard filters → candidate pool

Candidates = rows with `last_task_complete == True` AND token length ≤ 32,768 (so the
completion is never truncated away). This gives **6,387** of 10,000 rows — comfortably
more than the 5,000 needed, letting the final ranking do the rest of the work. (A
stricter filter additionally requiring `json_ok_frac ≥ 0.95` and zero autocorrects gives
5,351 rows — close to 5,000 — confirming these signals are consistent and that the
recipe has real room to select a clean top slice.)

## 5. Composite score (within the candidate pool)

```
score = json_ok_frac
        - 0.6 * autocorrect_rate
        - 0.1 * extra_text_after_rate
        - 0.1 * field_issue_rate
        - ppl_penalty(z_nll)          # 0.05*z + 0.3*max(0,z-1) + 0.3*max(0,-z-2)
        - 0.06 * max(0, z_turns)      # only penalizes above-average turn counts
```
(`z_*` = z-scores within the candidate pool.) Higher is better.

## 6. Diversity-aware ordering and group assignment

A max-heap greedily builds the final 5,000-row order: it repeatedly takes the
highest-scoring *not-yet-taken* row from any task-description cluster, so distinct tasks
are exhausted before a second attempt at the same task is ever added. This keeps
group 1 both high-scoring and broad-coverage rather than dominated by a few tasks with
many repeated high-quality attempts. The resulting order is chunked directly into groups
of 1,000 (rows 1–1000 → group 1, ..., 4001–5000 → group 5), so score is monotonically
non-increasing by construction across the group boundaries.

## 7. Result (sanity-checked post hoc)

| group | mean score | task_complete | json_ok | autocorrect/turn | mean turns | unique tasks |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1.059 | 100% | 1.000 | 0.000 | 16.7 | 801/1000 |
| 2 | 1.011 | 100% | 1.000 | 0.017 | 17.9 | 927/1000 |
| 3 | 0.976 | 100% | 1.000 | 0.027 | 18.5 | 966/1000 |
| 4 | 0.947 | 100% | 0.997 | 0.070 | 23.9 | 964/1000 |
| 5 | 0.898 | 100% | 0.985 | 0.245 | 30.0 | 979/1000 |

All 5 groups are far above the full-pool baseline task-completion rate (63.9%), and
quality degrades cleanly and monotonically from group 1 to group 5 on every underlying
signal (format cleanliness, harness auto-corrections, turn efficiency), which is what
should drive the benchmark-score ordering after training.

## Constraints respected

- Inference-only: only forward passes (`torch.no_grad`) of the frozen base model; no
  gradients/optimizer steps (also structurally blocked by `guards/sitecustomize.py`).
- No access to the benchmark/test set; all signals derived from `config.dataset_path`
  and the base model.
- `recipe/sft.py` was read only for context (chat template / masking / truncation
  behavior) and never executed or modified.

# Method

I read `config.yaml` and used its `base_model`, `dataset_path`, `n_groups`, `group_size`, and `max_len` values directly. I scored every trajectory with a composite value estimate designed for terminal-agent SFT.

The first component is a trajectory-quality heuristic: it rewards completed solutions, test/build evidence, code edits, useful shell exploration, recovery from errors, valid command-bearing assistant turns, and substantial assistant supervision. It penalizes handoff/timeout traces, repeated parsing problems, unfinished final turns, excessive install churn, and very short or runaway logs.

The second component is inference-only base-model NLL. I formatted each row as ChatML, masked loss to assistant turns, capped scoring sequences at `min(max_len, 2048)`, and ran only forward passes with the read-only base model. The loss contribution favors challenging-but-learnable examples: above-median assistant loss is useful, while the highest-loss noisy tail and very easy examples are discounted.

Rows were sorted by the combined score. The top 5000 rows were selected and split into 5 contiguous groups of exactly 1000; therefore group 1 contains the highest-valued subset and later groups monotonically receive lower-ranked samples.

Method

I read config.yaml and used its base_model, dataset_path, n_groups, group_size, and max_len values directly. I scored every trajectory with a composite value estimate designed for terminal-agent SFT.

The first component is a trajectory-quality heuristic: it rewards completed solutions, test/build evidence, code edits, useful shell exploration, recovery from errors, valid command-bearing assistant turns, and substantial assistant supervision. It penalizes handoff/timeout traces, repeated parsing problems, unfinished final turns, excessive install churn, and very short or runaway logs.

The second component is inference-only base-model NLL. I formatted each row as ChatML, masked loss to assistant turns, capped scoring sequences at min(max_len, 2048), and ran only forward passes with the read-only base model. The loss contribution favors challenging-but-learnable examples: above-median assistant loss is useful, while the highest-loss noisy tail and very easy examples are discounted.

Rows were sorted by the combined score. The top 5000 rows were selected and split into 5 contiguous groups of exactly 1000; therefore group 1 contains the highest-valued subset and later groups monotonically receive lower-ranked samples.

# Method

Read `config.yaml` and used `base_model=./model`, `dataset_path=./data/train.parquet`, `n_groups=5`, `group_size=1000`, and `max_len=32768`. I did not modify or run `recipe/sft.py`.

I ranked every trajectory with an inference-only value score aimed at terminal-agent SFT utility. The score rewards trajectories that end with `task_complete: true`, parse into the expected JSON action format, contain concrete shell commands, inspect and edit files, run verification commands such as test suites or linters, show late success evidence, and cover software/data/Linux task vocabulary. It penalizes advice-only transcripts, repeated JSON parsing failures, excessive protocol warnings, unresolved late errors, dangerous shell patterns, heavy repetition, and extreme transcript lengths that are likely to truncate or waste the fixed recipe context.

After scoring all rows, I selected the top `5000` rows with a small deterministic novelty adjustment over task-description terms to avoid filling the best groups with near-duplicate tasks. The selected rows are written in descending value order: group 1 receives the strongest `1000` rows, group 2 the next strongest, through group 5.

A second inference-only refinement scored the top candidate band with the read-only base model. For each candidate I rendered the full conversation with the model chat template, truncated to `2048` tokens (bounded by `max_len=32768`), computed next-token NLL under `torch.inference_mode()`, and averaged only tokens inside rendered assistant turns. This model signal was used conservatively as a reranking term: lower-NLL well-formed assistant behavior is favored, but the handcrafted terminal-agent quality score remains dominant.

# Selection method

I ranked every trajectory with a deterministic composite quality score designed for
terminal-agent SFT. The largest weights went to a clean final `task_complete: true`
state and success evidence in actual terminal output (for example, passing tests or a
successful build). I penalized unfinished final actions, unresolved-work language,
recent failing output, and malformed responses to the required JSON command protocol.

Smaller terms reward trajectories that both edit and verify code, provide a useful
amount of assistant supervision, and solve the task efficiently. I rendered every row
with the same chat template used by the fixed recipe and counted tokens exactly. Rows
longer than `max_len` were penalized because truncation can remove the verified solution
and train mostly on an unfinished prefix. This is an inference-free structural signal;
no model or proxy was trained and the SFT recipe was neither run nor modified.

I selected the 5,000 highest-scoring rows from the full candidate pool, sorted them by
descending score, and assigned consecutive blocks of 1,000 to group IDs 1 through 5.
Thus group 1 concentrates verified, protocol-compliant, non-truncated solutions, while
each later group has monotonically lower predicted SFT value.

# Selection method

I scored every trajectory using inference-only signals derived from the training data and the exact recipe constraints. The dominant signals were strict assistant-protocol validity, substantive shell actions, iterative file/code modification, test-command use, observed passing-test output, and explicit task completion. I gave smaller credit to useful multi-turn feedback and implementation-oriented tasks. I penalized parsing failures, unfinished trajectories, mostly `echo`/read-only activity, pathological loops, and estimated truncation beyond `max_len`.

This favors trajectories that teach the full terminal-agent loop—inspect, modify, run tests, interpret feedback, and finish—rather than answer-only transcripts or unverified claims. The top 5,000 rows by composite value were split into five contiguous score bands of 1,000, so group 1 contains the strongest subset and expected value decreases with group ID.

# Selection method

I ranked every trajectory with a deterministic terminal-agent utility score. The strongest signals were explicit successful completion and passing test/build feedback. Secondary positive signals were actual code/file edits, use of test commands, multiple command/observation turns, and a useful (but not excessive) amount of assistant supervision. I penalized unfinished or failing trajectories, protocol warnings, purely informational answers, very short examples, and trajectories truncated by the configured chat-template token limit.

Token lengths were measured with the recipe's generation-mask Qwen3 chat tokenizer and the configured `max_len`. I selected the top configured `n_groups × group_size` rows, then assigned consecutive score bands to groups, so group 1 contains the highest-valued rows and group 5 the lowest-valued selected rows. Exact score ties use test/coding evidence, length, and row index for deterministic ordering.
